newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to open more ports to China shipping - paper.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to open more ports to China shipping - paper.

text.p: A Taiwan cabinet agency has proposed widening an experiment in quasi-direct shipping exchanges with arch rival China to two more local ports, Taipei's China Times said on Tuesday.
The policymaking Mainland Affairs Council proposed allowing Taiwan's western port at Taichung and its main northern port at Keelung to participate in the exchanges, the paper said.
The newspaper, quoting unidentified sources, said Beijing in return may consider allowing more of the communist mainland's ports to operate direct routes to Nationalist-ruled Taiwan.

The China Times quoted sources as saying the Mainland Affairs Council was considering a further liberalisation in which limited direct exchanges of China and Taiwan cargoes would be allowed for the first time in 48 years.

In April, Taipei cautiously eased a ban dating to 1949 and allowed selected mainland and Taiwan companies to begin sailing direct routes between its southern port of Kaohsiung and two nearby mainland ports, Xiamen and Fuzhou.
Despite the breakthrough, the service remains restricted.

Incoming mainland cargoes cannot enter Taiwan customs and must be transshipped to third destinations. Likewise, Taiwan cargoes cannot be put aboard ships that will be crossing directly to the mainland.

Tens of thousands of Taiwan firms that have poured more than US$30 billion into mainland investments have pressured Taipei to allow direct cargo exchanges, saying transshipping them via Hong Kong as is now required adds unnecessary cost and delays.
Until April, Taipei had banned Taiwan Strait crossings since a 1949 civil war split that left communists in control of the mainland and the defeated Nationalists in exile on Taiwan.
Taipei remains reluctant to allow direct cargo exchanges, wary of weakening its political position against the communist government.
Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province that must eventually be brought under mainland rule.

Taipei accepts the idea of eventual reunification, but only after the Communist Party drops its monopoly on power and allows multiparty democracy. In the meantime, Taiwan allows unofficial economic and personal links with China but no official ties.
